title: Early voting in 2026 see surge in first few days across North Carolina - ABC11 News
text:
Vote 2026 NC | Early voting in North Carolina surges in first few days compared to 2022 - ABC11 Raleigh-Durham 
 24/7 Live Raleigh Durham Fayetteville Surrounding Area POLITICS 
 Early voting sites see surge in first few days across North Carolina 
 More than half a million North Carolina voters have already cast their ballots as of Saturday. By Tom George Monday, October 19, 2026 3:37AM Share Follow ABC11 on Google RALEIGH, N.C. (WTVD) -- More than half a million North Carolina voters have already cast their ballots as of Saturday as early voting continues ahead of the midterm election, with turnout running higher than at the same point in 2022.
 For the past five decades, Ren Pridgeon has been a familiar face at the polls in Raleigh. He began working elections in 1976, when he was 22 years old and Jimmy Carter was elected president.
 Since then, Pridgeon has seen changes in how people cast their ballots. After serving as an election judge and now as a volunteer, he has watched more voters choose to vote early.
 "What I say if you really want to vote, you vote, because no vote, means no voice," Pridgeon said.
 Fifty years later, Pridgeon said North Carolina has become a battleground receiving national attention.
 This year's high-stakes U.S. Senate race features former Gov. Roy Cooper and Michael Whatley. Pridgeon also hopes voters look beyond the top of the ticket.
 "So that's one of reasons I'm here is to educate people on the judges, and the councilmen and the commissioners that will lead North Carolina into the next couple of years, we need this," Pridgeon said.
 Voters at the polls Sunday said they recognized their ballots could help determine the balance of power in Washington.
 "It possibly could, it possibly could," one voter said.
 The economy was also top of mind for voters, with gas prices, food prices and education among the issues mentioned.
 Some voters seeking change said they supported Cooper, who has been leading consistently in the polls against Whatley.

 More than 500,000 voters statewide had already cast ballots, with early turnout running much higher than in 2022.
 Michael Bitzer, a professor at Catawba College, said Democratic enthusiasm could be contributing to the turnout.
 "Republicans are about flat in comparison to 2022 So that tells me that there is certainly energy and enthusiasm, at least in this early period. On the Democratic side, something that all the polls have picked up on throughout the year," Bitzer said.
 Republicans, meanwhile, are hoping to rally their base, with Vice President JD Vance scheduled to be in Hendersonville on Monday and President Donald Trump in Greenville on Tuesday.
 Despite the current Senate polls, Republicans are also hoping to have an impact on crucial U.S. House races. That includes North Carolina's 11th District in the western part of the state and the 1st District in eastern North Carolina, where Democratic Rep. Don Davis is in a tight race with Republican Laurie Buckhout.
 "Well, know, it certainly can't hurt on the Republican side to have the president come into the state and try and rally the troops. The big issue is, will Democrats then use that presidential visit to say, remember, everything that you don't like? He is here in persona kind of exemplifying it. So it's really a kind of double edged sword," Bitzer said.
 Not every county in North Carolina offered early voting Sunday, but both Wake and Durham counties did. Turnout in both counties was higher Sunday than at the same point in 2022.
 Final numbers are expected Monday.
